questions.title: Explain the React Virtual DOM and how reconciliation works.
questions.suggested_answer:
The Virtual DOM (VDOM) is a lightweight JavaScript in-memory representation of the actual DOM. When component state changes, React creates a new Virtual DOM tree and compares it with the previous snapshot using a heuristic O(n) diffing algorithm called Reconciliation.

Key aspects:
1. Element Type Check: If element types differ, React tears down the old subtree and mounts the new one.
2. Keys in Lists: Unique stable keys allow React to track elements across renders, minimizing DOM insertions and deletions.
3. Batching: React batches multiple state updates into a single render pass to avoid layout thrashing.
key_points: Virtual DOM is in-memory JavaScript representation of real DOM
Diffing algorithm operates in O(n) complexity rather than standard O(n^3) tree diffing
Keys are critical for list rendering performance
Batching groups DOM updates into single reflow
common_mistakes: Saying Virtual DOM is directly faster than real DOM (it adds overhead, but minimizes expensive layout reflows)
Using array index as key in dynamic lists that reorder
Failing to mention Fiber architecture and incremental rendering

How does React 18 automatic batching differ from earlier versions?

questions.title: What are ACID properties in relational database systems?
questions.suggested_answer:
ACID guarantees reliability in transactional database operations:

1. Atomicity: "All or nothing". Either the entire transaction succeeds, or it is rolled back completely.
2. Consistency: Transactions must take the database from one valid state to another, upholding all constraints, cascades, and rules.
3. Isolation: Concurrent transactions execute independently without interfering with each other (controlled via isolation levels like Read Committed, Repeatable Read, Serializable).
4. Durability: Once a transaction commits, its modifications are permanently recorded in non-volatile storage (WAL / Write-Ahead Log) even in system crash.
key_points: Atomicity prevents partial writes
Consistency enforces schema integrity constraints
Isolation avoids dirty reads and phantom reads
Durability utilizes Write-Ahead Logging
common_mistakes: Confusing Atomicity with Consistency
Assuming all transactions run with Serializable isolation by default
follow_up_questions: What are dirty reads, non-repeatable reads, and phantom reads?
How does Postgres implement isolation using MVCC (Multi-Version Concurrency Control)?

questions.title: How would you design a URL shortening service like Bitly or TinyURL?
questions.suggested_answer:
Designing a URL shortener requires addressing high-read throughput, URL uniqueness, and minimal redirect latency:

1. Requirements: Shorten long URL to 7-character string, redirect short URL to original destination, track click metrics.
2. Capacity: 100M URLs/month, 10:1 read-to-write ratio. 7-character Base62 string (a-z, A-Z, 0-9) provides 62^7 = ~3.5 trillion unique combinations.
3. Encoding: Counter / Snowflake ID converted to Base62, avoiding MD5/SHA256 collisions.
4. Architecture: Load Balancer -> Web API -> Redis Cache -> PostgreSQL / NoSQL.
5. Cache: Cache top 20% most accessed URLs in Redis with LRU eviction for sub-10ms redirection.
key_points: Base62 encoding (a-z, A-Z, 0-9) yields 3.5T unique 7-char keys
Distributed counter or Ticket Server prevents ID collision across microservices
Redis caching with LRU handles 80/20 read-heavy traffic
HTTP 301 vs 302: 301 caches in browser, 302 routes through server for analytics
common_mistakes: Using pure hash function without collision handling strategy
Forgetting HTTP 301 vs 302 distinction
follow_up_questions: Why would you pick 302 Temporary Redirect over 301 Moved Permanently if analytics are required?
How do you handle expired short URLs?

questions.title: Tell me about a time you had a technical disagreement with a team member and how you resolved it.
questions.suggested_answer:
Use the STAR method (Situation, Task, Action, Result):

"In my previous project, we were deciding whether to implement client-side state management with Redux or React Query for our dashboard. A senior engineer wanted Redux because of past familiarity, while I noticed our data was primarily server-state with caching and re-fetching needs.

Instead of debating opinions, I created a time-boxed 1-day spike comparing boilerplate, bundle size, and cache invalidation between both approaches. When we reviewed the metrics together, we saw React Query reduced our codebase by 40% while automatically providing background re-validation.

My colleague agreed with the data-driven recommendation, and we successfully delivered the feature ahead of schedule with zero state synchronization bugs."
key_points: Use the STAR framework (Situation, Task, Action, Result)
Focus on objective data, prototypes, and team outcomes rather than winning an argument
Show professional respect and active listening
common_mistakes: Blaming the other person or sounding defensive
Leaving out the concrete result or lessons learned
follow_up_questions: What would you have done if the team chose the alternative approach anyway?

questions.title: How do you design a high-throughput URL shortener like bit.ly?
questions.suggested_answer: To design a URL shortener, compute an MD5 or SHA-256 hash or use a distributed counter (Snowflake/base62 encoding) to generate a 7-character slug. Store key-value mappings in a distributed NoSQL key-value store (like DynamoDB/Cassandra) with a Redis cache layer for the top 20% hot links. Use Rate limiting with Token Bucket to prevent scraping.
key_points: Base62 encoding of an auto-incrementing ID (62^7 combinations)
Distributed cache (Redis) fronting the persistent database
Handling hash collisions vs base62 sequence IDs
Read-heavy caching strategy (80/20 rule)
common_mistakes: Using relational single-node DB with auto-increment without sharding
Forgetting redirection HTTP status codes (301 vs 302)
follow_up_questions: How do you handle custom alias URLs?
How do you handle expired links and cleanup?

questions.title: What is the difference between SQL and NoSQL databases, and how do you choose?
questions.suggested_answer: SQL databases (PostgreSQL, MySQL) are relational, table-based, ACID-compliant, and excel at complex joins and transactional consistency. NoSQL databases (MongoDB, Cassandra, Redis) are non-relational, document or key-value stores with flexible schemas designed for horizontal scalability and high throughput. Choose SQL for finance/e-commerce orders and NoSQL for sensor telemetry, chat logs, or cache.
key_points: ACID vs BASE consistency models
Horizontal vs vertical scalability
Structured vs dynamic schema
Read/write patterns and join overhead
common_mistakes: Claiming NoSQL is always faster than SQL
Ignoring PostgreSQL JSONB support
follow_up_questions: When would you use a hybrid polyglot persistence architecture?

questions.title: Tell me about a time you had a technical disagreement with a teammate.
questions.suggested_answer: Use the STAR method: Situation: During an API migration, a teammate favored GraphQL while I recommended REST with OpenAPI due to our team's existing monitoring tooling. Task: We needed to deliver within 3 weeks without breaking downstream consumers. Action: We scheduled a 30-minute spike, built small prototypes of both, and evaluated latency, caching simplicity, and client adoption costs together. Result: We agreed on REST with OpenAPI, delivered 2 days ahead of deadline with zero regression bugs.
key_points: Focus on facts and technical prototypes rather than ego
Seek consensus aligned with project constraints
Acknowledge the merit of the other person's proposal
Deliver measurable positive outcomes
common_mistakes: Blaming or portraying the coworker negatively
Saying you have never had a disagreement
follow_up_questions: What would you do if your manager made a technical decision you strongly disagree with?

questions.title: Explain CSS Specificity, the Box Model, and BEM methodology.
questions.suggested_answer: The CSS box model consists of content, padding, border, and margin. Box-sizing: border-box includes padding and border in width/height. Specificity determines which rules apply: Inline styles (1000) > IDs (100) > Classes/Attributes/Pseudo-classes (10) > Elements/Pseudo-elements (1). BEM (Block Element Modifier) provides structured naming like .btn, .btn__icon, .btn--primary to prevent specificity wars.
key_points: box-sizing: border-box vs content-box
Calculation weights: inline, ID, class, tag
BEM structure avoiding deeply nested selectors
common_mistakes: Overusing !important to bypass specificity
Confusing margin collapsing
follow_up_questions: How does CSS Grid differ from Flexbox?

questions.title: What is Database Indexing, and how do B-Trees and Hash Indexes work?
questions.suggested_answer: An index is a data structure (commonly B-Tree or B+Tree) that improves data retrieval speed at the expense of additional writes and storage. B-Trees maintain sorted keys with log(N) lookup, range scans, and insertions. Hash indexes provide O(1) equality lookup but do not support range queries.
key_points: B-Tree vs Hash index trade-offs
Clustered index vs secondary indexes
Index selectivity and composite index column order
Write amplification during INSERT/UPDATE
common_mistakes: Adding indexes on every single column indiscriminately
Not knowing that leading columns matter in composite indexes
follow_up_questions: What is an index scan vs an index-only scan?

questions.title: How does JWT authentication work and how do you handle token revocation?
questions.suggested_answer: JSON Web Tokens contain Header, Payload, and Signature encoded in base64. The server verifies the signature using a secret/public key without querying a database (stateless). Because JWTs cannot be revoked natively until expiration, best practice is short-lived access tokens (15 mins) paired with rotating refresh tokens stored in HTTP-only cookies and tracked in Redis for immediate revocation.
key_points: Header, Payload, Signature breakdown
Stateless verification benefit
Token revocation strategy via Redis blocklist or refresh token rotation
Storing tokens in secure HTTP-only SameSite cookies vs LocalStorage
common_mistakes: Storing sensitive passwords or secrets inside JWT payload (payload is only base64 encoded, not encrypted)
Making access tokens valid for 30 days without revocation
follow_up_questions: How does OAuth 2.0 differ from standard JWT auth?

questions.title: Why do you want to work for our company and what are your long-term goals?
questions.suggested_answer: Tie your response to the company's specific product, engineering culture, and domain impact. Emphasize how your technical skills in building production systems align with their roadmap, and articulate a desire to grow into a senior engineer who champions clean architecture, automated testing, and mentorship.
key_points: Specific knowledge of company's tech stack and mission
Mutual growth alignment
Focus on technical excellence and collaboration
common_mistakes: Giving a generic copy-paste answer that applies to any company
Focusing solely on compensation and perks
follow_up_questions: Where do you see yourself in 3 years?

questions.title: How do WebSockets differ from HTTP Polling and Server-Sent Events (SSE)?
questions.suggested_answer: HTTP Polling involves repeated requests with high overhead. Long-polling holds connections open until data arrives. SSE (Server-Sent Events) is unidirectional (server-to-client) over standard HTTP, ideal for live feeds and AI streaming. WebSockets provide full-duplex, bidirectional, low-latency communication over a single TCP connection, ideal for chat and multiplayer gaming.
key_points: Unidirectional vs bidirectional communication
TCP handshake and protocol upgrade (ws://)
SSE auto-reconnection and HTTP/2 multiplexing support
Connection scaling and load balancer sticky sessions
common_mistakes: Using WebSockets when simple SSE or polling would suffice
Forgetting heartbeat pings/pongs to detect dropped connections
follow_up_questions: How do you scale WebSocket connections across multiple server instances?
